sentences.text: Wamweracaudia was a large quadrupedal herbivore belonging to the sauropod lineage.
Researchers believe one vertebra is missing from the known series of tail bones.
The authors identified four unique derived traits, known as autapomorphies, for this species.
The upper surface of the front and middle tail vertebrae is excavated at the rear.
The neural processes of the front tail vertebrae have a rough zone on the upper third of the side surface separated from the rear rough zone by a vertical groove.
The underside of the middle to rear vertebrae is strongly pinched transversely, forming a ridge rather than a flat surface.
A pair of small extensions called tubercula is present on the top rib facet of the front tail vertebrae between the prezygapophysis and diapophysis.

Research by Beeston et al. in 2026 indicates that Wamweracaudia keranjei exhibits pneumaticity in its anterior caudal vertebrae, a trait showing at least five independent origins or reversals in Neosauropoda.
The genus name Wamweracaudia combines the name of the Wamwera tribe with the Latin word for tail.
The species name keranjei honors Mohammadi Keranje, the foreman who led the excavation team.
Wamweracaudia lived 155 to 145 million years ago in the Late Jurassic of Tanzania, Africa.
A sauropod tail was excavated at Site G during German expeditions to Tendaguru between 1909 and 1912 under the supervision of Werner Janensch.
Werner Janensch referred the tail to Gigantosaurus robustus in 1929.
The tail was assigned to the separate genus Janenschia in 1991.
The specimen was named Wamweracaudia keranjei in 2019 by Mannion, Upchurch, Schwarz, and Wings.
The holotype consists of specimens MB.R.2091.1–30, MB.R.3817.1, and MB.R.3817.2 found in the Tithonian layer of the Tendaguru Formation.
There are two recorded fossil occurrences of Wamweracaudia.
Wamweracaudia is classified within the dinosaur class Saurischia.
Cladistic analysis places Wamweracaudia in the family Mamenchisauridae as a sister species of Mamenchisaurus.
Wamweracaudia and Mamenchisaurus share procoelous tail vertebrae.
Wamweracaudia belongs to the family Mamenchisauridae.
Wamweracaudia lived during the Tithonian stage, between 149.2 and 143.1 million years ago.
It is debated whether two additional traits are autapomorphies, pending confirmation that Wamweracaudia is a mamenchisaurid.
